accepted.question: Explain six points about threat classes and the countermeasures used against attacks, covering how threats differ from vulnerabilities and attacks, how misuse detection counters known attacks, and how anomaly-based prediction counters unknown activity.

marking_points.point: A threat is only a potential violation of security, whereas an attack is the actual violation.

marking_points.point: An attack is defined as the actual violation of security, distinguishing it from a mere threat.
marking_points.quote: Attacks: The actual violation of security

marking_points.point: A vulnerability is a weakness of a system that can be exploited to damage assets.
marking_points.quote: Vulnerabilities: Weakness of a system that can be exploited to damage assets

marking_points.point: Misuse detection represents attacks as patterns or signatures so that variations of the same attack can be detected.
marking_points.quote: there are ways to represent attacks in the form of a pattern or a signature so that even variations of the same attack can be detected

marking_points.point: Misuse detection is effective against known attack patterns but of little use against unknown attack methods.
marking_points.quote: They can detect many or all known attack patterns, but they are of little use for unknown attack methods.

marking_points.point: Predictive pattern anomaly detection can flag anomalous activities that traditional methods found difficult to detect.
marking_points.quote: Rule based sequential patterns can detect anomalous activities that were difficult with traditional methods.

questions.question: Explain three Windows security mechanisms or components described in the lecture and, for each, one security concern that arises from it.

marking_points.point: Windows provides complex mechanisms for managing user accounts, objects and access control.
marking_points.quote: Windows systems contain complex security mechanisms for user account and object management as well as access control.

marking_points.point: Discretionary access control (DACS) allows fine-grained control over diverse entities in Windows and its applications.
marking_points.quote: DACS enable ﬁne-grained access control of heterogeneous entities in Windows itself as well as applications.

marking_points.point: The same complexity that gives Windows strong security also makes it vulnerable, since misconfiguration and implementation bugs can cause serious incidents.
marking_points.quote: The complexity of Windows security mechanisms is also its enemy: misconﬁguration as well as implementation bugs may lead to severe security incidents.

marking_points.point: Active Directory, introduced in Windows 2000, is an LDAP-like directory service used to organize system resources.
marking_points.quote: Active directory introduced in Windows 2000 is an LDAP-like directory service for organization of system resources:

marking_points.point: Active Directory stores security credentials and certificates as part of its directory information.
marking_points.quote: Security credentials and certiﬁcates

marking_points.point: Windows subjects are processes and threads, and their security credentials are held in a token that is inherited when new processes are created.
marking_points.quote: Security credentials for a subject are stored in a token.

questions.question: Explain six points about threat classes and the countermeasures used against attacks, covering how threats differ from vulnerabilities and attacks, how misuse detection counters known attacks, and how anomaly-based prediction counters unknown activity.

marking_points.point: A threat is only a potential violation of security, whereas an attack is the actual violation.
marking_points.quote: Threats: A threat is a                                                          “potential” violation of                                                                    security

marking_points.point: An attack is defined as the actual violation of security, distinguishing it from a mere threat.
marking_points.quote: Attacks: The actual                                                                               violation of security

marking_points.point: A vulnerability is a weakness of a system that can be exploited to damage assets.
marking_points.quote: Vulnerabilities: Weakness of a system that can be exploited to damage assets

marking_points.point: Misuse detection represents attacks as patterns or signatures so that variations of the same attack can be detected.
marking_points.quote: there are ways to represent attacks in the form of a pattern or a signature so that even variations of the same attack can be detected

marking_points.point: Misuse detection is effective against known attack patterns but of little use against unknown attack methods.
marking_points.quote: They can detect many or all known attack patterns, but they are of little use for unknown attack methods.

marking_points.point: Predictive pattern anomaly detection can flag anomalous activities that traditional methods found difficult to detect.
marking_points.quote: Rule based sequential patterns can detect anomalous activities that were difficult with traditional methods.

questions.question: Explain how a substitution cipher works and what serves as its key.

marking_points.point: Encryption replaces each plaintext letter with a different letter to produce the ciphertext.
marking_points.quote: In substitution ciphers, we replace the plain-text letters with other letters

marking_points.point: The substitution rule itself functions as the key of the cipher.
marking_points.quote: The substitution rule is the key

questions.question: State six techniques by which malware attacks systems or propagates, including how a virus infects executable files and how a worm spreads.

marking_points.point: A virus can append its body to a host program and redirect the program's entry point to the virus code.
marking_points.quote: Append a virus body to a program

marking_points.point: After running, the virus restores the original entry point and transfers control back to it.
marking_points.quote: Virus code restores the original                                 entry point and jumps to it after                                     its own execution

marking_points.point: A virus can overwrite a program header so that execution begins at the virus instead of the original code.
marking_points.quote: Over write a program header to switch the entry point to a virus

marking_points.point: A worm can propagate by exploiting a remote execution feature of a network service such as sendmail.
marking_points.quote: Used a debugging feature of sendmail (remote execution)

marking_points.point: A rootkit hides malicious processes and software so the attacker keeps privileged remote access after a vulnerability is exploited.
marking_points.quote: Rootkits are a type of malware that mask malicious processes and software in the infected systems to ensure privileged remote access.

marking_points.point: Spyware steals user credentials and records activity such as keystrokes and visited sites.
marking_points.quote: They steal user logins and passwords, document sites visited, log keystrokes and even redirect browsers to unwanted sites.

questions.question: Explain the Chinese Wall model's purpose and its two access rules.

marking_points.point: The Chinese Wall policy was proposed by Brewer and Nash to address conflicts of interest.
marking_points.quote: Brewer and Nash (1989) proposed a policy called the Chinese Wall Policy that addresses such conflicts of interest.

marking_points.point: The simple security rule allows access only to objects within the same company datasets already accessed or in an entirely different conflict of interest class.
marking_points.quote: A subject s can be granted access to an object o only if the object: is in the same company datasets as the objects already accessed by s, that is, “within the Wall,” or belongs to an entirely different conflict of interest class.

questions.question: Discuss six aspects of biometric mechanisms and technologies, covering their definition, categories, and the strengths and weaknesses of specific biometric methods.

marking_points.point: A biometric is defined as a physiological or behavioural characteristic that can distinguish one person from another and can be used for identification or verification.
marking_points.quote: A biometric is a physiological or behavioural characteristic of a human being that can distinguish one person from another and that theoretically can be used for identification or verification of identity.

marking_points.point: Biometric applications are categorized into two sectors: psychological and behavioural.
marking_points.quote: Biometric applications available today are categorized into 2 sectors

marking_points.point: The psychological category includes iris, fingerprints, hand, retinal and face recognition.
marking_points.quote: Psychological: Iris, Fingerprints, Hand, Retinal and Face recognition

marking_points.point: The behavioural category includes voice, typing pattern and signature.
marking_points.quote: Behavioural: Voice, Typing pattern, Signature

marking_points.point: Retinal scanning is very efficient and cannot be spoofed, but has disadvantages such as high failure-to-enrol ratio, acceptability concerns, light exposure and hygiene.
marking_points.quote: Very efficient – cant be spoofed!

marking_points.point: Fingerprint biometrics suffer from disadvantages including racial issues, dirt, grime and wounds, placement of finger, large database processing, and spoofing concerns.
marking_points.quote: Racial issues

questions.question: Explain how a professional code of ethics guides computing professionals, referring to the ACM code and ACM professional conduct.

marking_points.point: A code of ethics is a documented set of acceptable behaviours for a professional group.
marking_points.quote: Documented set of acceptable behaviors for professional or social groups.

marking_points.point: The code is defined by the professional group itself.
marking_points.quote: Defined by the group.

marking_points.point: The code identifies which specific actions are appropriate or inappropriate.
marking_points.quote: Identifies specific actions as appropriate or inappropriate.

marking_points.point: The ACM code requires professionals to contribute to society and human well-being, treating all people as stakeholders.
marking_points.quote: Contribute to society and to human well-being, acknowledging that all people are stakeholders in computing.

marking_points.point: The ACM code requires professionals to respect privacy and honour confidentiality.
marking_points.quote: Respect privacy.

marking_points.point: ACM professional conduct requires professionals to give comprehensive and thorough evaluations of computer systems and their impacts, including possible risks.
marking_points.quote:
Give comprehensive and thorough evaluations of                                                    computer systems and
their impacts, including analysis of possible risks.

questions.question: Refer to your answer in (a). Explain six preventive network security mechanisms, other than the NIDS, that an organization can deploy to protect its network, and state what each mechanism does.

marking_points.point: A firewall controls incoming and outgoing network traffic according to predetermined security policies.
marking_points.quote: Control incoming and outgoing traffic on network with predetermined security policies.

marking_points.point: A proxy server improves data security and network performance by acting as a firewall and web filter, providing shared connections and caching data.
marking_points.quote: Proxy servers act as a firewall and web filter, provide shared network connections, and cache data to speed up common requests.

marking_points.point: Network segmentation creates boundaries between segments whose computing assets share a common function, risk or role.
marking_points.quote: Boundaries between network segments where computing assets within the segment have a common function, risk or role within an organization.

marking_points.point: A remote access VPN gives individual hosts or clients secure remote access to the organization's network.
marking_points.quote: Provides remote and secure access to an organization network to individual hosts or clients

marking_points.point: Zero Trust Network Access limits each user to only the access and permissions needed for their role.
marking_points.quote: A user should only has access and permission that required to fulfill the role

marking_points.point: An intrusion detection/prevention system detects or prevents attacks such as brute force, denial-of-service and exploitation of network vulnerabilities.
marking_points.quote: To detect or prevent the network security attacks such as brute force attacks, Denial-of-Service attacks and exploits of network vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Describe six (6) aspects of Kerberos and single sign-on mechanisms, covering their motivation, design criteria, login procedure and alternatives.

marking_points.point: Single sign-on reduces the need for users to memorize passwords.
marking_points.quote: Reduce the need to memorize passwords

marking_points.point: Single sign-on reduces the time spent typing passwords.
marking_points.quote: Reduce the time spent on typing passwords

marking_points.point: Kerberos is designed to be secure against eavesdropping by never transmitting passwords in clear text.
marking_points.quote: Security against eavesdropping: no                                       password transmission in clear text.

marking_points.point: Kerberos is designed for transparency, so the user is unaware of any authentication beyond the initial login.
marking_points.quote: Transparency: user is not aware of any                            authentication beyond an initial login.

marking_points.point: During Kerberos login, the hash of the user's password becomes the secret key of the client/user.
marking_points.quote: The hash value of his password                                                      KU = h(P) becomes a secret key of the                                                  client/user.

marking_points.point: Alternative authentication mechanisms to passwords include smart cards, biometric methods and two-factor authentication.
marking_points.quote: Alternative user authentication mechanisms are smart cards, biometric methods and two-factor authentication.

questions.question: State six facts about the Samy worm and the XSS attack it used, covering how the script was injected, how it spread, and the outcome.

marking_points.point: The worm injected JavaScript into a user profile using document.body.innerHTML.
marking_points.quote: Inject Javascript into a user proﬁle using document.body.innerHTML

marking_points.point: It obtained the list of the user's heroes by issuing a GET on a user profile.
marking_points.quote: Get the list of user’s heros by using a GET on a user proﬁle

marking_points.point: It added Samy as a friend field by performing XML-HTTP on the addFriends page.
marking_points.quote: Add Samy as a ﬁeld by performing XML-HTTP on the addFriends page

marking_points.point: Any user visiting an infected user's page had their profile and friends list infected with the JavaScript.
marking_points.quote: Any user who visits an infected user’s page will gets proﬁle infected with Javascript and his friends list infected with Samy

marking_points.point: The infection eventually reached about 1,000,000 MySpace profiles.
marking_points.quote: Eventually about 1,000,000 MySpace proﬁles were infected.

marking_points.point: The underlying XSS flaw is that any web application returning user input without filtering is a potential XSS vulnerability.
marking_points.quote: Any web application that returns user input without ﬁltering is a potential XSS vulnerability!
